The Battle of Bannockburn. On the twenty-third and twenty-fourth of June, thirteen fourteen, Robert the Bruce, king of Scotland, led his forces to one of medieval warfare's greatest upsets. Near the River Bannock south of Stirling Castle, a Scottish army of eight to twelve thousand defeated an English invasion force of roughly twenty thousand troops led by Edward II.

Robert the Bruce was a military strategist of extraordinary skill. He positioned his troops on a bog and steep terrain that rendered the English numerical advantage and cavalry superiority entirely useless. The Scottish formation called the schiltron—tightly packed pikemen bristling with long spears—proved devastatingly effective against cavalry charges. Wave after wave of English mounted knights broke against this formation and were cut down.

The English defeat forced Edward II to abandon the invasion entirely. By thirteen twenty-eight, through the Treaty of Edinburgh, Scotland's independence was officially recognised. The victory became the defining symbol of Scottish national identity and established Robert the Bruce as a legendary figure in Scottish history. He was the architect of national independence, the man who refused to accept English feudal suzerainty and secured his kingdom's freedom through military genius and unflinching determination. The battle remains celebrated as one of the greatest strategic victories in medieval military history, a triumph of terrain, discipline, and unshakeable will.
